name: Denon AVR-S770H
summary: A 7.2-channel Denon with 8K-ready HDMI and HEOS streaming that can run a full 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos layout, but its basic Audyssey MultEQ and 75 W rating suit efficient speakers in small to medium rooms.
verdict:
The AVR-S770H has **seven amplified channels**, so the maths is simple: five ear-level speakers plus two height speakers is seven, which gives you a complete **5.1.2 Dolby Atmos** system, or 7.1 with no heights. It cannot reach 5.1.4 or 7.1.4, and there are no main-channel pre-outs for adding an amp later.

Denon rates it at **75 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.08% THD, 2 ch driven)**. That two-channel figure is the best case. With all seven channels busy, they share one power supply, so real multichannel output is lower. Here is why that rarely matters in a normal room: loudness at 1 m = sensitivity + 10 × log10(watts). A 90 dB [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) speaker fed 75 W reaches about 108.8 dB at 1 m, or roughly 99 dB at a seat 3 m away. Halve the power and you lose only 3 dB. With 85 dB speakers, that same seat tops out near 94 dB, which is loud but short of reference peaks.

Room correction is entry-level [Audyssey MultEQ](/glossary/room-correction/), not MultEQ XT or XT32. If you want finer EQ, the [Denon AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/) is the next step up. See the full ranking in our [best home theater receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) guide.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the AVR-S770H and AVR-X1800H?
faqs.a: Both are 7.2-channel receivers. The X1800H adds Audyssey MultEQ XT for finer room correction and a slightly higher 80 W/ch rating. The power gain is about 0.3 dB, so the real reason to step up is the better EQ, not loudness.

name: Denon AVR-X1800H
summary: The sweet-spot Denon for a 5.1.2 Atmos room: Audyssey MultEQ XT, 8K-ready HDMI and HEOS streaming in a 7.2-channel box that is easy to set up.
verdict:
The AVR-X1800H looks like a small step over the [AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/): **80 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.08% THD, 2 ch driven)** against 75 W. Do the maths and the power gain is 10 × log10(80 ÷ 75) = **0.28 dB**, which nobody can hear. The reason to pay more is room correction.

The X1800H uses **Audyssey MultEQ XT**, which applies far finer filters than basic MultEQ. That matters most below about 300 Hz, where room modes cause the boomy peaks and dips you hear in most living rooms. Better [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/) will change the sound more than any 0.3 dB of extra headroom.

Channel count is the same: **seven amplified channels**, so you get 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos or 7.1, not 5.1.4. Remember that the rating is for two channels driven. With seven speakers playing a loud action scene, each channel gets less than 80 W, but with 88 dB speakers a 40 W peak still gives about 104 dB at 1 m and roughly 94.5 dB at a 3 m seat.

If you want a second HDMI output for a projector, look at the [AVR-X2800H](/gear/denon-avr-x2800h/). For the full field, see our [best home theater receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) picks.

faqs.q: Is 80 watts per channel enough for a home theater?
faqs.a: For most rooms, yes. With speakers rated 88 dB or higher, 80 W gives around 107 dB at 1 m, which is still loud at a 3 m seat. If your speakers are rated 85 dB or lower, or your room is large, consider a 9-channel model with more headroom.

name: Denon AVR-X2800H
summary: A 7.2-channel Denon with 95 W/ch, Audyssey MultEQ XT and two HDMI outputs, ideal if you run both a TV and a projector from one 5.1.2 system.
verdict:
The AVR-X2800H is still a **seven-channel** receiver, so like the [AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/) it powers 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos or 7.1, not 5.1.4. What you pay for is a second HDMI output and a little more power.

Denon rates it at **95 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.08% THD, 2 ch driven)**. Compared with 80 W, that is 10 × log10(95 ÷ 80) = **0.75 dB** more headroom. Useful with less sensitive speakers, but not a different class of loudness. The two-channel rating also overstates what you get with seven channels running together: a shared power supply means each channel sees less on a busy movie mix.

The practical maths for a projector room: a 12 ft seat is about 3.7 m, which costs about 11.3 dB versus 1 m. With 87 dB speakers at 95 W, you get roughly 106.8 dB at 1 m and about 95.5 dB at the seat. That is comfortable movie level with a [subwoofer](/best-subwoofer-for-home-theater/) taking the bass below the [crossover](/glossary/crossover/).

The second HDMI output is the real reason to buy it: run a TV for daytime and a projector for movies without swapping cables. If you want nine channels for 5.1.4, the [AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/) is the next stop.

name: Denon AVR-X3800H
summary: Nine amplified channels, 11.4-channel processing, four independent sub outputs and Audyssey XT32 with a Dirac Live upgrade path make this the best-value receiver for a serious 5.1.4 or 7.1.4 room.
verdict:
The AVR-X3800H is where channel maths gets interesting. It has **nine amplified channels** and **11.4-channel processing**. Nine amps run **5.1.4** (five ear-level, four height) or **7.1.2**. Add a two-channel power amp such as the [Marantz MM7025](/gear/marantz-mm7025/) to the pre-outs and you reach **7.1.4**: 7 + 4 = 11 channels, with the receiver powering nine.

Denon rates it at **105 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.05% THD, 2 ch driven)**. As with every receiver, the two-channel figure is the ceiling, not what each of nine channels gets on a full-range blast. Offloading the front left and right to an external amp frees the internal supply for the other seven, which is the practical way to get more real multichannel headroom.

The bass side is strong: **four independent subwoofer outputs** let you place and level each sub separately, which smooths seat-to-seat response far better than one sub. [Room correction](/glossary/room-correction/) is Audyssey MultEQ XT32, with **Dirac Live** available as a paid upgrade.

It also decodes [DTS:X](/glossary/dts-x/), [Dolby Atmos](/glossary/dolby-atmos/), Auro-3D and IMAX Enhanced. For a 5.1.4 room it is hard to beat; compare it with rivals in the [best home theater receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) guide.

name: Denon AVR-X4800H
summary: The X3800H's 9.4-channel, 11.4-processing platform with 125 W/ch and more HDMI inputs, for larger rooms or less sensitive speakers.
verdict:
The AVR-X4800H shares the key layout of the [AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/): **nine amplified channels**, **11.4-channel processing**, and four independent subwoofer outputs. Nine amps give you 5.1.4 or 7.1.2, and adding a two-channel amp takes you to 7.1.4.

The headline difference is power: **125 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.05% THD, 2 ch driven)** against 105 W. Run the numbers: 10 × log10(125 ÷ 105) = **0.76 dB**. That is a modest gain. The bigger benefit is a stronger amp section and power supply, which helps when you push nine channels hard in a large room.

Here is a room check. With 86 dB speakers and a 4 m seat (about 12 dB of distance loss from 1 m), 125 W gives roughly 86 + 21 = 107 dB at 1 m and about 95 dB at the seat. That is fine for most viewers, but if you aim for reference peaks with low-sensitivity [speakers](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/), an external amp for the fronts is still the smarter upgrade.

You also get Audyssey MultEQ XT32, a paid Dirac Live upgrade, and 8 HDMI inputs. If your room and speakers are average, the X3800H delivers nearly the same result for less. Compare both in our [best home theater receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) guide.

name: Marantz Cinema 60
summary: A full-size 7.2-channel Marantz rated at 100 W/ch with Audyssey MultEQ XT and HEOS, a good fit for a 5.1.2 system with mid-sensitivity speakers.
verdict:
The Cinema 60 is a **seven-channel** receiver, so the layout options are 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos or 7.1. What it adds over slimline and budget receivers is power.

Marantz rates it at **100 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.08% THD, 2 ch driven)**, double the 50 W/ch rating common on slimline models. Doubling power buys **3 dB** of headroom. In a room with 87 dB speakers and a 3 m seat, that moves peak level from about 94.5 dB to about 97.5 dB. Worth having, but remember the test is two channels driven: with seven speakers working at once, the shared supply gives each one less than the label suggests.

Against the [Denon AVR-X2800H](/gear/denon-avr-x2800h/), the maths is close: 100 W vs 95 W is about 0.2 dB, and both use Audyssey MultEQ XT [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/). The choice comes down to Marantz's styling and voicing versus the Denon's lower price and dual HDMI outputs.

You get HEOS, AirPlay 2 and 8K-ready HDMI. What you do not get is a ninth channel: if you want 5.1.4, step up to the [Marantz Cinema 50](/gear/marantz-cinema-50/). For more options, see the [best home theater receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) roundup.

name: Marantz Cinema 50
summary: Marantz's 9.4-channel receiver with 11.4 processing, four independent sub outputs, Audyssey XT32 and a Dirac Live upgrade, for a 5.1.4 room with a path to 7.1.4.
verdict:
The Cinema 50 has **nine amplified channels** and **11.4-channel processing**. That means 5.1.4 or 7.1.2 straight out of the box, and 7.1.4 once you add a two-channel power amp on the pre-outs. Seven ear-level plus four height is eleven speakers; the receiver powers nine and the external amp handles two.

Marantz rates it at **110 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.05% THD, 2 ch driven)**. Against the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/) at 105 W, the difference is 10 × log10(110 ÷ 105) = **0.2 dB**. These two share the same core feature set: 11.4 processing, four independent subwoofer outputs, Audyssey MultEQ XT32 and an optional **Dirac Live** license. The Marantz costs more for its styling, front-panel design and house voicing.

The bass management is the hidden strength. Four independent sub outputs let you run two to four [subwoofers](/best-subwoofer-for-home-theater/) and set each one's distance and level, which evens out the room modes that make bass boom at one seat and vanish at the next.

As always, the two-channel rating is the best case. For loud 7.1.4 playback, moving the front pair to an external amp frees the internal supply for the rest. Compare it with the Denon in our [best home theater receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) guide.

name: Yamaha RX-V4A
summary: A 5.2-channel Yamaha with MusicCast streaming and YPAO calibration that decodes Atmos but has no channels for real height speakers.
verdict:
Count the amps first: the RX-V4A has **five amplified channels**. That is a 5.1 system: left, center, right and two surrounds, plus a subwoofer. There are no spare channels for height speakers, so while it decodes [Dolby Atmos](/glossary/dolby-atmos/) and DTS:X, it can only render them virtually through Dolby Atmos Height Virtualization. If you want physical 5.1.2, you need seven channels, which means the [Yamaha RX-V6A](/gear/yamaha-rx-v6a/) or a Denon 7.2 model.

Yamaha rates it at **80 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.06% THD, 2 ch driven)**. In a 5.1 system that is a reasonable match for bookshelf speakers. With 87 dB speakers, 80 W gives about 87 + 19 = 106 dB at 1 m, or roughly 96.5 dB at a 3 m seat. Remember the two-channel test: with five speakers playing at once, each gets less, so lean on a powered sub with an 80 Hz [crossover](/glossary/crossover/) to unload the amps.

You get YPAO [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/), MusicCast multiroom, AirPlay 2 and 8K-ready HDMI on four inputs. It suits a small living room that will stay 5.1. For more options at this price, see our [best budget home theater receiver](/best-budget-home-theater-receiver/) guide.

name: Yamaha RX-V6A
summary: A 7.2-channel Yamaha rated at 100 W/ch with seven HDMI inputs, YPAO and MusicCast, a solid 5.1.2 Atmos receiver with a generous power rating for the money.
verdict:
The RX-V6A has **seven amplified channels**, so it runs a real **5.1.2 Dolby Atmos** system: five ear-level speakers, two height speakers and a subwoofer. That is the key upgrade over the five-channel [RX-V4A](/gear/yamaha-rx-v4a/).

Yamaha rates it at **100 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.06% THD, 2 ch driven)**. Against Denon's 80 W [AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/), that is 10 × log10(100 ÷ 80) = **about 1 dB** more headroom. In a room with 87 dB speakers and a 3 m seat, 100 W gives roughly 107 dB at 1 m and about 97.5 dB at the seat. The usual caveat applies: the test drives two channels, and seven channels playing a loud scene share the same supply.

Where the Denon pulls ahead is [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/). Yamaha's YPAO is simpler than Audyssey MultEQ XT, so bass control in an awkward room is weaker. On the other hand, seven HDMI inputs is generous at this price, and MusicCast, AirPlay 2 and Spotify Connect cover streaming.

One note: owners report that early units had a 4K/120 HDMI chipset problem with some consoles, which Yamaha addressed with a free upgrade. See where it lands in the [best budget home theater receiver](/best-budget-home-theater-receiver/) list.

name: Yamaha AVENTAGE RX-A4A
summary: Yamaha's 7.2-channel AVENTAGE model with 110 W/ch, Surround:AI and MusicCast, built for 5.1.2 Atmos in a sturdier chassis than the RX-V line.
verdict:
The RX-A4A is a **seven-channel** receiver, so it powers 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos or 7.1, the same layout as the cheaper [RX-V6A](/gear/yamaha-rx-v6a/). The AVENTAGE badge buys a more rigid chassis, extra features like Surround:AI, and a bit more rated power.

Yamaha rates it at **110 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.06% THD, 2 ch driven)**. Against the RX-V6A's 100 W, that is 10 × log10(110 ÷ 100) = **0.4 dB**. Against Denon's 95 W [AVR-X2800H](/gear/denon-avr-x2800h/), it is about 0.6 dB. So, you are not buying loudness. With 87 dB speakers and a 3 m seat, all three land within about 1 dB of 97.5 dB peak. And with seven channels working together, the two-channel rating overstates what each speaker gets.

Surround:AI is the feature owners talk about: it analyzes scenes and adjusts the sound field automatically. Room correction is YPAO, which is simpler than Audyssey MultEQ XT or Dirac. If your room has strong bass modes, better [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/) will matter more than the extra watts.

The RX-A4A makes sense if you like Yamaha's sound and want the sturdier AVENTAGE build. If you want nine channels at a similar price, look at the [Onkyo TX-RZ50](/gear/onkyo-tx-rz50/).

name: Sony STR-AN1000
summary: A 7.2-channel Sony with 360 Spatial Sound Mapping, Chromecast and AirPlay 2, whose headline power figure uses generous test conditions you need to read carefully.
verdict:
The STR-AN1000 has **seven amplified channels**, so it runs 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos or 7.1. Sony adds **360 Spatial Sound Mapping**, which uses the speakers you have to create phantom speakers and widen the sound field.

Now the power maths. Sony's headline is **165 W/ch (6 Ω, 1 kHz, 10% THD, 1 ch driven)**. Each of those conditions makes the number bigger than you would see in real use:

- **6 Ω instead of 8 Ω** draws more current, so more watts.
- **1 kHz only**, not the full 20 Hz–20 kHz band where bass demands the most power.
- **10% THD** is well into audible clipping. Most receivers here are rated at 0.05–0.08%.
- **One channel driven**, so the power supply feeds a single amp, not seven.

The result is that 165 W cannot be compared with Denon's or Yamaha's figures. Treat the AN1000 as a normal 7.2 receiver and do the room maths with efficient speakers: [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) of 88 dB or more and a seat within about 3.5 m.

The strengths are elsewhere: D.C.A.C. IX auto calibration, Chromecast built-in, AirPlay 2 and 8K-ready HDMI. It is a strong choice for Sony TV owners. Compare it with the [Denon AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/) in our [best home theater receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) guide.

name: Sony STR-DH590
summary: A low-cost 5.2-channel receiver with 4K HDR pass-through and Bluetooth for a basic 5.1 system, without Dolby Atmos, Wi-Fi or 4K/120.
verdict:
The STR-DH590 is about the cheapest way into a real **5.1** speaker system. It has **five amplified channels** and two subwoofer outputs, which covers left, center, right and two surrounds. It does not decode Dolby Atmos or DTS:X, so there is no height option at all.

Sony rates it at **145 W/ch (6 Ω, 1 kHz, 10% THD, 1 ch driven)**. Read those conditions closely. A 6 Ω load draws more current than 8 Ω, a 1 kHz tone skips the bass that eats amp power, 10% THD is audible clipping, and one channel driven means the power supply is not shared. Those numbers are not comparable with the 8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, two-channel ratings Denon and Yamaha use.

So plan the system around efficient speakers. With 88 dB [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) bookshelf speakers in a small room, a modest amp still reaches comfortable movie levels, especially if a powered sub takes everything below an 80 Hz [crossover](/glossary/crossover/).

The HDMI side is basic: **4 inputs, 1 output**, 4K HDR pass-through but no 8K or 4K/120, so a PS5 or Xbox Series X should connect to the TV instead. Bluetooth is built in; Wi-Fi is not. If you can stretch, the [Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/) adds Atmos and modern HDMI. More options are in our [best budget home theater receiver](/best-budget-home-theater-receiver/) guide.

name: Onkyo TX-NR6100
summary: A THX Certified Select 7.2-channel receiver rated at 100 W/ch with Chromecast and AirPlay 2, sized for 5.1.2 rooms around 2,000 cubic feet.
verdict:
The TX-NR6100 has **seven amplified channels**, so it runs 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos or 7.1. Onkyo rates it at **100 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.08% THD, 2 ch driven)**, a little more than Denon's 80 W [AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/): 10 × log10(100 ÷ 80) is about **1 dB** of extra headroom.

The more useful number is the **THX Certified Select** badge. THX Select is aimed at rooms of about **2,000 cubic feet** with a seat around 10–12 ft from the screen. Do the room maths: 15 × 17 ft with an 8 ft ceiling is 2,040 cu ft, a typical large living room or modest dedicated room. If your space is close to that, the certification says the receiver can reach THX's target levels there with suitable speakers.

As always, the power rating is two channels driven. Seven speakers sharing the supply in a loud scene get less each, so a powered sub crossed at 80 Hz (see [crossover](/glossary/crossover/)) is important.

Room correction is Onkyo's AccuEQ with AccuReflex, which is simpler than Audyssey MultEQ XT. You do get Chromecast built-in, AirPlay 2 and 8K-ready HDMI. For a nine-channel Onkyo with Dirac Live, step up to the [TX-RZ50](/gear/onkyo-tx-rz50/). See the [best home theater receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) guide for more.

name: Onkyo TX-NR5100
summary: An affordable 7.2-channel Onkyo with 80 W/ch, Chromecast and AirPlay 2 that covers a basic 5.1.2 Atmos system, with simpler room correction than Denon rivals.
verdict:
The TX-NR5100 has **seven amplified channels**, enough for **5.1.2 Dolby Atmos** or 7.1. It is Onkyo's answer to the [Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/).

Onkyo rates it at **80 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.08% THD, 2 ch driven)**. Against the Denon's 75 W, that is 10 × log10(80 ÷ 75) = **0.28 dB**, which you will not hear. So compare them on features, not watts. Remember that the rating is for two channels driven: a seven-channel Atmos scene shares one power supply, so real per-channel output is lower.

Here is the room check. With 88 dB speakers, 80 W gives about 88 + 19 = 107 dB at 1 m, or about 97.5 dB at a 3 m seat. That is plenty for a living room if a powered [subwoofer](/best-budget-subwoofer-for-home-theater/) handles the [LFE](/glossary/lfe/) channel and the bass below 80 Hz.

Room correction is AccuEQ, which handles basic levels and distances but offers less bass control than Audyssey. You do get Chromecast built-in, AirPlay 2 and 8K-ready HDMI. If the price gap is small, the [Onkyo TX-NR6100](/gear/onkyo-tx-nr6100/) adds THX certification and about 1 dB more rated power.

name: Onkyo TX-RZ50
summary: A 9.2-channel THX Certified Select receiver with Dirac Live included, the most affordable way here to get nine amplified channels and top-tier room correction in one box.
verdict:
The TX-RZ50 has **nine amplified channels**, so it can power **5.1.4** (five ear-level speakers and four heights) or **7.1.2** without an external amp. That is two more channels than any 7.2 receiver, and it is where Atmos starts to sound like sound is moving overhead instead of coming from two points above you.

Onkyo rates it at **120 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.08% THD, 2 ch driven)**. Against the 105 W [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/), that is 10 × log10(120 ÷ 105) = **0.6 dB**. With nine speakers playing at once, every receiver delivers less than its two-channel rating, so the real gap is small either way.

The big advantage is **Dirac Live** [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/) included in the box. Dirac is widely regarded as one of the most capable correction systems for bass and timing. On the Denon, it costs extra.

Where the Denon wins: 11.4-channel processing and four independent sub outputs, which matter if you plan 7.1.4 or multiple subwoofers. The RZ50 has **two** sub outputs and processes nine channels. THX Certified Select means it targets rooms around 2,000 cu ft. For a 5.1.4 room that size, compare it with the Denon in our [best home theater receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) guide.
